name: Question 5
problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=yz-x.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,-1,1).$
worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,-1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(0,-1,1)+∇f(0,-1,1)\cdot ⟨x,y+1,z-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(0,-1,1)=-1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =-1\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(0,-1,1)=-1, \\ {f}_{y} & =z\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(0,-1,1)=1, \\ {f}_{z} & =y\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(0,-1,1)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(0,-1,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(0,-1,1) & =⟨{f}_{x}(0,-1,1),{f}_{y}(0,-1,1),{f}_{z}(0,-1,1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(0,-1,1)+∇f(0,-1,1)\cdot ⟨x,y+1,z-1⟩ \\  & ≈-1+⟨-1,1,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x,y+1,z-1⟩ \\  & ≈-1-(x)+(y+1)-(z-1) \\  & ≈1-x+y-z.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Let f(x,y,z)=yz−x. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (0,−1,1).

a
f(x,y,z)≈2x+y
b
f(x,y,z)≈−2+2y+3z
c
f(x,y,z)≈−3+2x−y+z
d
f(x,y,z)≈1−x+y−z
e
 f(x,y,z)≈−x−y−2z
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b,c) is given by f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)⋅⟨x−a,y−b,z−c⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (0,−1,1) is f(x,y,z)≈f(0,−1,1)+∇f(0,−1,1)⋅⟨x,y+1,z−1⟩.

From the definition of f, we have that f(0,−1,1)=−1. Computing the partial derivatives, we get fx=−1⇒fx(0,−1,1)=−1,fy=z⇒fy(0,−1,1)=1,fz=y⇒fz(0,−1,1)=−1.

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point (0,−1,1) is given by ∇f(0,−1,1)=⟨fx(0,−1,1),fy(0,−1,1),fz(0,−1,1)⟩=⟨−1,1,−1⟩.

Finally, the linear approximation of the function f is f(x,y,z)≈f(0,−1,1)+∇f(0,−1,1)⋅⟨x,y+1,z−1⟩≈−1+⟨−1,1,−1⟩⋅⟨x,y+1,z−1⟩≈−1−(x)+(y+1)−(z−1)≈1−x+y−z.
